title: Calcium, magnesium and phosphate
subtitle: Corrected calcium, arrhythmia risk and refeeding patterns
summary: Corrected calcium, arrhythmia risk and refeeding patterns
introduction: Use the reporting laboratory range. Corrected calcium formulas are approximations and become unreliable in critical illness, major acid–base disturbance, severe hypoalbuminaemia and renal failure; ionised calcium is preferable in these settings.

rows.name: Hypocalcaemia
notes: Consider vitamin D deficiency, hypoparathyroidism, renal failure, pancreatitis, sepsis, low magnesium or massive transfusion. Symptoms include perioral tingling, carpopedal spasm, tetany, seizure and prolonged QT.

rows.name: Hypercalcaemia
notes: Consider malignancy, primary hyperparathyroidism, medication or granulomatous disease. Look for dehydration, constipation, vomiting, polyuria, confusion, weakness and shortened QT.

rows.name: Magnesium
notes: Low magnesium can cause tremor, weakness, seizures, hypokalaemia that is difficult to correct and ventricular arrhythmias including torsades. High magnesium can cause hyporeflexia, bradycardia, hypotension and respiratory depression.

rows.name: Phosphate
notes: Low phosphate can cause weakness, respiratory muscle failure, rhabdomyolysis and haemolysis. A rapid fall after nutrition in a malnourished patient suggests refeeding syndrome, often with low potassium and magnesium.

calculations.title: Approximate corrected calcium
interpretation: They become unreliable in critical illness, major acid–base disturbance, severe hypoalbuminaemia and renal failure; ionised calcium is preferable in these settings.

parityCases.description: Albumin 40 g/L leaves measured calcium unchanged.

inputs.label: Measured calcium (mmol/L)
inputs.validationMessage: Enter measured calcium between 0.5 and 5.0 mmol/L.

urgentFindings: Tetany, seizure, stridor, prolonged QT or arrhythmia with suspected hypocalcaemia.
Corrected calcium around ≥3.0 mmol/L with dehydration, vomiting, confusion, weakness or ECG change.
Severe hypomagnesaemia with ventricular arrhythmia, seizure or persistent hypokalaemia.
Low phosphate with respiratory weakness, profound generalised weakness, rhabdomyolysis or suspected refeeding syndrome.
overrides: Use the reporting laboratory’s reference ranges and compare with previous results, symptoms, observations, medication and fluid status.

commonPatterns.title: Hypocalcaemia driven by low magnesium
findings: Magnesium also below the normal range
Hypocalcaemia not correcting despite calcium replacement
interpretation: Magnesium is required for parathyroid hormone release and action; hypomagnesaemia commonly causes or perpetuates hypocalcaemia that will not correct until magnesium is also replaced
actions: Request magnesium alongside calcium if not already done, and replace magnesium as part of the correction plan (see further testing)
Look for a cause of magnesium loss: diuretics, alcohol, malabsorption, poor intake or proton-pump inhibitor use
Treat as time-critical if tetany, seizure, stridor, prolonged QT or arrhythmia is present (see urgent findings)

commonPatterns.title: Possible malignancy-related hypercalcaemia
findings: Corrected calcium raised, particularly if markedly so
Weight loss, bone pain, known or suspected malignancy, or new confusion/dehydration
interpretation: Malignancy (via bony metastases or PTH-related peptide) is a common cause of significant hypercalcaemia, particularly when the rise is marked or rapid, and often carries a different urgency and work-up to primary hyperparathyroidism
actions: Assess hydration status, confusion, weakness and any known cancer history
Treat as time-critical if corrected calcium is around ≥3.0 mmol/L with symptoms or ECG change (see urgent findings)
Arrange medical review for further work-up, including PTH and consideration of the underlying malignancy (see further testing)

commonPatterns.title: Refeeding syndrome picture
findings: Phosphate falling rapidly, often with low potassium and low magnesium
Recent reintroduction of nutrition (oral, enteral or parenteral) after a period of malnutrition, prolonged fasting or minimal intake
interpretation: Reintroducing carbohydrate drives an insulin surge that shifts phosphate, potassium and magnesium intracellularly, producing this combined pattern — it is a recognised, preventable cause of cardiac and respiratory complications
actions: Identify at-risk patients before or as soon as feeding starts: prolonged poor intake, alcohol excess, significant weight loss, or unwell/malnourished older adults
Request potassium and magnesium alongside phosphate to confirm the combined pattern (see further testing)
Treat as time-critical if there is respiratory or generalised weakness, rhabdomyolysis, or the picture is severe (see urgent findings)

commonPatterns.title: Renal-failure mineral pattern
interpretation: Reduced renal phosphate excretion raises phosphate, which in turn suppresses calcium and can drive secondary hyperparathyroidism over time — a different mechanism to the low-phosphate refeeding pattern above
actions: Correlate with U&E/eGFR to confirm the degree of renal impairment and whether it is acute or chronic
Request PTH if the derangement is persistent or the diagnosis is unclear (see further testing)
Arrange medical review for renal function assessment and management planning

commonPatterns.title: Symptomatic derangement with arrhythmia risk
findings: Marked abnormality of calcium, magnesium or phosphate
Palpitations, syncope, seizure, tetany or generalised weakness
interpretation: Calcium and magnesium derangements directly affect cardiac conduction (QT prolongation/shortening, torsades) and neuromuscular excitability; symptoms should be taken seriously even before the precise cause is established
actions: Obtain a 12-lead ECG and look specifically for QT change or arrhythmia (see further testing)
Treat as time-critical per the relevant urgent finding and do not wait for the full biochemical picture before escalating a symptomatic patient (see urgent findings)
Check potassium alongside calcium/magnesium/phosphate, as combined electrolyte disturbances are common and compound arrhythmia risk

rationale: Renal function is central to interpreting calcium, magnesium and phosphate disturbances and to identifying a renal cause or contraindication to treatment
Distinguishes primary hyperparathyroidism from other causes of hypercalcaemia, and supports assessment of hypocalcaemia when hypoparathyroidism is suspected
Identifies QT prolongation/shortening or arrhythmia associated with significant calcium or magnesium derangement, particularly in a symptomatic patient
Deficiency is a common and treatable contributor to hypocalcaemia, particularly alongside a low or low-normal phosphate

Needed to calculate corrected calcium; also a reminder that the correction becomes unreliable in severe hypoalbuminaemia, critical illness or major acid–base disturbance, when ionised calcium is preferable
Relevant when severe hypophosphataemia raises concern for rhabdomyolysis or significant muscle weakness
